newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen hijacker eludes police after hostage-drama.
newsitem.headline: Chechen hijacker eludes police after hostage-drama.

text.p: Police in southern Russia said on Tuesday they were still searching for a lone Chechen hijacker who held dozens of hostages on a bus in the ethnic region of Dagestan before fleeing alone over the border into Chechnya.
But officials told Russian news agencies they had little hope of tracking down the man in the breakaway province, which is largely under the control of separatist rebels.
Monday evening's brief hijacking in the Dagestan capital Mackachkala appeared to have no direct link to the conflict in Chechnya, where a fragile truce has been holding for a month.
The 24-year-old man, who identified himself to hostages as Ruslan, said he was a daring Chechen guerrilla.
But his claim to have taken part in two bloody separatist raids across Chechnya's borders, including one into Dagestan last January, sounded flimsy and his main aim appeared to be money.
After seizing the bus with, by various accounts, 35 to 48 people aboard he threatened to detonate two hand grenades and a can of petrol unless given $100,000 and a helicopter.
Dagestan's interior minister was quoted by Interfax news agency as saying he told hostages all his family had been killed by Russian troops in Chechnya and he had nothing to lose.
But little more than an hour later, having driven to the airport, the man released all but three hostages and agreed to leave with a local Dagestan politician in the latter's car.
Interfax said the man had accepted a reduced cash offer of 100 million roubles -- about $18,500.

The politician, Gadzhi Makhachev, told Itar-Tass news agency they had driven to the Chechen border near the Dagestan town of Khasavyurt -- some 100 km (60 miles) west of Makhachkala -- where the man simply got out and walked across the frontier.
Makhachev said he had persuaded the man to take a drink with him first -- he preferred beer to vodka -- and so had managed to take a set of fingerprints from the glass.

But Interfax quoted a Russian security official as saying there was little chance of an effective search for the hijacker in Chechnya. Dagestan police told Tass they were still searching their own region in case the man had returned.
Initial reports of the hijacking stirred memories of January's raid on the Dagestan town of Kizlyar when Chechen guerrillas led by Salman Raduyev took hundreds of hostages.
They then withstood days of Russian air and artillery bombardment in the village of Pervomaiskoye, near Khasavyurt, before escaping back across the Chechen border.
But the hijacking more vividly recalled several other incidents in the volatile North Caucasus region in recent years.
On September 20, 1995, two hijackers demanded $1.5 million and a helicopter after seizing a bus in Makhachkala. Police stormed it, arresting the men and freeing all 18 hostages.

In May 1994, four Chechens were arrested after hijacking a school bus near Vladikavkaz and flying four of the hostages by helicopter with them back to Chechnya. A month later, three gunmen were captured as they tried to flee with their ransom after holding a busload of passengers near Mineralniye Vody.
In December 1993, police arrested four men in Makhachkala, freeing teenagers seized at a school in the southern Russian city of Rostov and flown by helicopter across the region.
